questions.question: An LP in nonnegative variables has a nonempty feasible region and a finite optimal value. What does corner point optimality guarantee?
options: Every feasible corner point attains the optimal value.
Only feasible corner points can attain the optimal value.
At least one feasible corner attains the optimal value.
The origin, as a corner point, attains the optimal value.

questions.question: An LP of the course type has exactly one optimal solution. What kind of point must it be?
options: A feasible corner point of the region
A point strictly inside the region
A boundary point that is not a corner
Any intersection of two boundary lines

questions.question: How does corner point optimality help when solving an LP with a finite optimum by hand?
options: Every feasible point must be tested, but in a cleverly chosen order.
Only the feasible corners need comparing, not every feasible point.
It is enough to evaluate the objective at a single feasible corner.
It shows the optimum lies at the corner closest to the origin.

questions.question: A student evaluates the objective of a maximization LP at all feasible corners and takes the best one, without checking anything else. Which condition of corner point optimality is being skipped?
options: That the best corner lies on an axis
That the best corner has whole-number values
That a finite optimal value exists at all
That all corners have different values

questions.question: An LP has a bounded feasible region and more than one optimal solution. What follows about its corner points?
options: Exactly one of its corner points is then optimal.
Every one of its corner points is optimal.
None of its corner points can be optimal.
At least two of its corner points are optimal.

questions.question: Giapetto's feasible region has corners $(0,0)$, $(40,0)$, $(40,20)$, $(20,60)$ and $(0,80)$, where $x_s$ and $x_t$ are weekly soldiers and trains. Where is $3x_s+2x_t$ maximized, and with what value?
options: At $(20,60)$, with value 180
At $(40,20)$, with value 160
At $(30,40)$, with value 170
At $(40,0)$, with value 120

questions.question: The bounded region $x_1+x_2\le6$, $x_1\le4$, $x_2\le5$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ has corners $(0,0)$, $(4,0)$, $(4,2)$, $(1,5)$ and $(0,5)$. What is the maximum of $2x_1+3x_2$ over it?
options: 17, at the corner $(1,5)$
15, at the corner $(0,5)$
14, at the corner $(4,2)$

questions.question: Minimize $3x_1+2x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\ge4$, $x_1+3x_2\ge6$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$. The region is unbounded, its corners are $(0,4)$, $(3,1)$ and $(6,0)$, and the minimum is finite. What is the optimum?
options: $(3,1)$, with cost 11
$(0,4)$, with cost 8
$(6,0)$, with cost 18
$(0,0)$, with cost 0

questions.question: For maximize $x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\le6$, $x_1\le4$, $x_2\le5$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$, the point $(3,3)$ is optimal with value 6, and it is not a corner point. What follows?
options: $(3,3)$ must be the unique optimal solution.
$(3,3)$ cannot be optimal, not being a corner.
$(3,3)$ cannot be the only optimal solution.
No corner of this region reaches the value 6.

questions.question: The region $x_1+x_2\le6$, $x_1\le4$, $x_2\le5$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ has corners $(0,0)$, $(4,0)$, $(4,2)$, $(1,5)$ and $(0,5)$. Which corners maximize $2x_1+2x_2$?

Maximize $x_1-x_2$ subject to $x_1-x_2\le2$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$. The optimal value is 2, attained at every point $(2+t,t)$ with $t\ge0$, and the corners are $(0,0)$ and $(2,0)$. Why does this not contradict the two-optimal-corners statement?
options: That statement assumes a bounded region, and this region is unbounded.
The LP has no finite optimum, so corner point optimality does not apply.
Both corners are optimal here, since each gives an objective value of 2.
The points $(2+t,t)$ are not feasible, so $(2,0)$ is the only optimum.

questions.question: Which statement follows from corner point optimality for an LP of the course type?
options: Every optimal solution of the LP is one of its corner points.
If a non-corner point is optimal, other optima exist as well.
If some corner is optimal, it is the only optimal solution.
A point that is not a corner can never be an optimal solution.

questions.question: After evaluating a maximization LP at all its feasible corners, a student finds the best value 30. What else must be known to conclude that the optimal value is 30?
options: That the corners were listed in some order
That only one corner achieves the value 30
That the origin is one of the feasible corners
That the LP has a finite optimal value at all

questions.question: Maximize $x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1-x_2\le2$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$. The feasible corners are $(0,0)$ and $(2,0)$, with values 0 and 2. What is the optimal value?
options: 2, attained at the feasible corner point $(2,0)$
0, attained at the feasible corner point $(0,0)$
4, attained at the feasible point $(3,1)$ only
None, since $(t,t)$ is feasible for all $t\ge0$

questions.question: Maximize $5x_1+4x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\le5$, $2x_1+x_2\le8$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$. Using the feasible corners, what is the optimum?
options: $(3,2)$, with value 23
$(4,0)$, with value 20
$(0,5)$, with value 20
$(0,8)$, with value 32

questions.question: Minimize $x_1+2x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\ge3$, $x_1\le2$, $x_2\le4$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$. The feasible corners are $(0,3)$, $(0,4)$, $(2,4)$ and $(2,1)$. What is the optimum?
options: $(0,3)$, with cost 6
$(0,4)$, with cost 8
$(2,1)$, with cost 4
$(3,0)$, with cost 3

questions.question: Maximize $x_1$ subject to $x_1\le3$, where $x_1\ge0$ but $x_2$ may take any real value. The optimal value 3 is attained at every point $(3,x_2)$. Why does this not contradict corner point optimality?
options: The optimum is not finite, so the result does not apply.
The point $(3,0)$ is a corner point, and it is optimal.
The region is empty, so the result does not apply here.
With $x_2$ free, the region has no corner point at all.

questions.question: For an LP of the course type with a bounded feasible region, consider (A): it has multiple optimal solutions, and (B): at least two of its corner points are optimal. How are A and B related?
options: A implies B, while B can hold without multiple optima.
B implies A, while A can hold with one optimal corner.
A implies B and B implies A, so they are equivalent.
Neither one implies the other in general.

questions.question: The bounded region $x_1+x_2\le6$, $x_1\le4$, $x_2\le5$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ has corners $(0,0)$, $(4,0)$, $(4,2)$, $(1,5)$, $(0,5)$. For maximize $cx_1+x_2$, the non-corner point $(2.5,3.5)$ is optimal. What is $c$?

For maximize $2x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\le4$, $x_1\le3$, $x_2\le3$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$, a student evaluates the objective at every intersection of two boundary lines and reports $(3,3)$ with value 9. What is the correct optimum?
options: $(3,0)$, with value 6
$(3,1)$, with value 7
$(4,0)$, with value 8
$(3,3)$, with value 9
